claim: Prostate cancer is the second most occurring cancer in men worldwide.
source: Prostate cancer is the second most occurring cancer in men worldwide.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract without supporting data or citations in the manuscript itself, but represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: A total of 488 prostate samples were used to build patient-specific models.
source: A total of 488 prostate samples were used to build patient-specific models and compared to available clinical data.
evidence: The manuscript describes the use of 488 TCGA samples in the methods and results sections.

claim: Eight prostate cell line-specific models were built to validate the approach with dose-response data.
source: Additionally, eight prostate cell line-specific models were built to validate our approach with dose-response data of several drugs.
evidence: The manuscript describes building models for eight cell lines from GDSC data.

claim: 15 actionable points of interventions were identified in one cell line-specific model whose inactivation hinders tumorigenesis.
source: We identified 15 actionable points of interventions in one cell line-specific model whose inactivation hinders tumorigenesis.
evidence: The abstract states this finding based on the model simulations.

claim: Nine small molecule inhibitors of five putative targets were tested experimentally.
source: To validate these results, we tested nine small molecule inhibitors of five of those putative targets and found a dose-dependent effect on four of them, notably those targeting HSP90 and PI3K.
evidence: The abstract describes experimental validation with specific numbers of inhibitors tested.

claim: Drugs targeting HSP90 and PI3K showed dose-dependent effects on LNCaP cell viability.
source: To validate these results, we tested nine small molecule inhibitors of five of those putative targets and found a dose-dependent effect on four of them, notably those targeting HSP90 and PI3K.
evidence: The abstract and experimental results sections describe dose-dependent effects of these drugs.

claim: Not all prostate patients respond to treatments in the same way, depending on the stage and type of their tumour.
source: Not all prostate patients respond to the treatments in the same way, depending on the stage and type of their tumour (Chen and Zhou, 2016) and differences in their genetic and epigenetic profiles (Toth et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The high heterogeneity of prostate cancer profiles can be explained by a large number of interacting proteins and complex cross-talks between cell signalling pathways.
source: The high heterogeneity of these profiles can be explained by a large number of interacting proteins and the complex cross-talks between the cell signalling pathways that can be altered in cancer cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about cancer biology based on established knowledge.

claim: Continuous mathematical modelling does not scale up well to large signalling networks due to difficulty of estimating kinetic parameter values.
source: Although continuous mathematical modelling has been widely used to study cellular biochemistry dynamics (e.g. ordinary differential equations) (Goldbeter, 2002; Kholodenko et al., 1995; Le Novère, 2015; Sible and Tyson, 2007; Tyson et al., 2019), this formalism does not scale up well to large signalling networks, due to the difficulty of estimating kinetic parameter values (Babtie and Stumpf, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Boolean models describe each protein as a binary variable (ON/OFF).
source: In particular, Boolean models, the simplest implementation of logical models, describe each protein as a binary variable (ON/OFF).
evidence: This is a definition of Boolean models based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Boolean modelling has been successfully used to describe the dynamics of human cellular signal transduction and gene regulations.
source: In the last years, logical and, in particular, Boolean modelling has been successfully used to describe the dynamics of human cellular signal transduction and gene regulations (Calzone et al., 2010; Cho et al., 2016; Flobak et al., 2015; Grieco et al., 2013; Helikar et al., 2008; Traynard et al., 2016) and their deregulation in cancer (Fumiã and Martins, 2013; Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: MaBoSS associates transition rates for activation and inhibition of each node of the network, enabling it to account for different time scales of processes.
source: In practice, MaBoSS associates transition rates for activation and inhibition of each node of the network, enabling it to account for different time scales of the processes described by the model.
evidence: This describes the technical features of the MaBoSS software used in the study.

claim: MaBoSS applies a Monte-Carlo kinetic algorithm (or Gillespie algorithm) to the STG to produce time trajectories.
source: Given some initial conditions, MaBoSS applies a Monte-Carlo kinetic algorithm (or Gillespie algorithm) to the STG to produce time trajectories (Stoll et al., 2017; Stoll et al., 2012) such that the time evolution of the model state probabilities can be estimated.
evidence: This describes the computational method used by MaBoSS, supported by citations.

claim: The prostate Boolean model was built upon a generic cancer Boolean model by Fumiã and Martins, 2013.
source: The model was built upon a generic cancer Boolean model by Fumiã and Martins, 2013, which integrates major signalling pathways and their substantial cross-talks.
evidence: This describes the foundation of the model construction, supported by citation.

claim: The initial generic network was extended to include prostate cancer-specific genes (e.g. SPOP, AR, etc.).
source: This initial generic network was extended to include prostate cancer-specific genes (e.g. SPOP, AR, etc.), pathways identified using ROMA (Martignetti et al., 2016), OmniPath (Türei et al., 2021), and up-to-date literature.
evidence: This describes the model construction process using multiple data sources.

claim: ROMA was applied to TCGA transcriptomics data using gene sets from cancer pathway databases.
source: ROMA was applied to the TCGA transcriptomics data using gene sets from cancer pathway databases (Appendix 1, Section 1.1.3, Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This describes a specific analysis performed on TCGA data.

claim: The final network includes 133 nodes and 449 edges.
source: The final model accounts for 133 nodes and 449 edges (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1, and in GINsim format at the address: http://ginsim.org/model/signalling-prostate-cancer).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the final model structure.

claim: The model has nine inputs (EGF, FGF, TGF beta, Nutrients, Hypoxia, Acidosis, Androgen, TNF alpha, and Carcinogen).
source: This model has nine inputs (EGF, FGF, TGF beta, Nutrients, Hypoxia, Acidosis, Androgen, TNF alpha, and Carcinogen presence) and six outputs (Proliferation, Apoptosis, Invasion, Migration, (bone) Metastasis, and DNA repair).
evidence: This describes the structure of the Boolean model.

claim: The model has six outputs (Proliferation, Apoptosis, Invasion, Migration, (bone) Metastasis, and DNA repair).
source: This model has nine inputs (EGF, FGF, TGF beta, Nutrients, Hypoxia, Acidosis, Androgen, TNF alpha, and Carcinogen presence) and six outputs (Proliferation, Apoptosis, Invasion, Migration, (bone) Metastasis, and DNA repair).
evidence: This describes the structure of the Boolean model.

claim: Healthy cells mostly exhibit quiescence (neither proliferation nor apoptosis) in the absence of any input.
source: These healthy cells mostly exhibit quiescence (neither proliferation nor apoptosis) in the absence of any input (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a simulation result from the wild type model shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When Nutrients and growth factors (EGF or FGF) are present, Proliferation is activated.
source: When Nutrients and growth factors (EGF or FGF) are present, Proliferation is activated (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a simulation result from the model shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Androgen is necessary for AR activation and helps in the activation of Proliferation.
source: Androgen is necessary for AR activation and helps in the activation of Proliferation, even though it is not necessary when Nutrients or growth factors are present.
evidence: This describes the model behavior under different input conditions.

claim: Cell death factors (such as Caspase 8 or 9) trigger Apoptosis in the absence of SPOP.
source: Cell death factors (such as Caspase 8 or 9) trigger Apoptosis in the absence of SPOP, while Hypoxia and Carcinogen facilitate apoptosis but are not necessary if cell death factors are present (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a simulation result from the model shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Invasion is activated by either β-catenin or a combination of CDH2, SMAD, or EZH2.
source: Invasion is first activated by known pro-invasive proteins: either β-catenin (Francis et al., 2013) or a combination of CDH2 (De Wever et al., 2004), SMAD (Daroqui et al., 2012), or EZH2 (Ren et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the model logic for invasion, supported by citations.

claim: Migration is activated by Invasion and EMT and with either AKT or AR.
source: Migration is then activated by Invasion and EMT and with either AKT or AR (Castoria et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the model logic for migration, supported by citation.

claim: Metastasis is activated by Migration and one of three nodes: RUNX2, ERG or ERG fused with TMPRSS2, FLI1, ETV1 or ETV4.
source: Lastly, (bone) Metastasis is activated by Migration and one of three nodes: RUNX2 (Altieri et al., 2009), ERG (Adamo and Ladomery, 2016) or ERG fused with TMPRSS2 (St John et al., 2012), FLI1, ETV1 or ETV4 (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2015).
evidence: This describes the model logic for metastasis, supported by citations.

claim: 488 individual Boolean models were constructed, one for each TCGA patient.
source: We tailored the generic prostate Boolean model to a set of 488 TCGA prostate cancer patients (Appendix 1, Section 4, Appendix 1—figure 9) using our personalisation method (PROFILE) (Béal et al., 2019), constructing 488 individual Boolean models, one for each patient.
evidence: This describes the personalization process applied to TCGA data.

claim: Personalised models were built using mutations, CNA and RNA expression data.
source: Personalised models were built using three types of data: discrete data such as mutations and copy number alterations (CNA) and continuous data such as RNAseq data.
evidence: This describes the data types used for model personalization.

claim: The phenotype DNA_repair separates low and high Gleason scores.
source: The phenotype DNA_repair, which can be interpreted as a sensor of DNA damage and genome integrity which could lead to DNA repair, seems to separate low and high Gleason scores (Figure 4A and Appendix 1, Section 4.1, Appendix 1—figures 15–18), confirming that DNA damage pathways are activated in patients (Marshall et al., 2019) but may not lead to the triggering of apoptosis in this model (Appendix 1, Section 4.1, Appendix 1—figure 11).
evidence: This is an observation from the personalized model simulations shown in Figure 4A, supported by citation.

claim: The density of high Proliferation score tends to increase as the Gleason score increases.
source: We then looked at the profiles of the phenotype scores across patients and their Gleason grade and found that the density of high Proliferation score (close to 1, Figure 4B) tends to increase as the Gleason score increases (from low to intermediate to high) and these distributions are significantly different (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, p-value = 0.00207; Appendix 1, Section 4.1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the personalized model simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Proliferation score distributions across Gleason grades are significantly different (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, p-value = 0.00207).
source: We then looked at the profiles of the phenotype scores across patients and their Gleason grade and found that the density of high Proliferation score (close to 1, Figure 4B) tends to increase as the Gleason score increases (from low to intermediate to high) and these distributions are significantly different (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, p-value = 0.00207; Appendix 1, Section 4.1).
evidence: This is a statistical test result from the data analysis.

claim: The Apoptosis phenotype probabilities do not have a clear trend across grades.
source: The Apoptosis phenotype probabilities, however, do not have a clear trend across grades (Figure 4C), even though the distributions are significantly different (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, p-value = 2.83E-6; Appendix 1, Section 4.1).
evidence: This is an observation from the personalized model simulations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Apoptosis score distributions across Gleason grades are significantly different (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, p-value = 2.83E-6).
source: The Apoptosis phenotype probabilities, however, do not have a clear trend across grades (Figure 4C), even though the distributions are significantly different (Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test, p-value = 2.83E-6; Appendix 1, Section 4.1).
evidence: This is a statistical test result from the data analysis.

claim: MYC_MAX complex and SPOP were identified as suitable points of intervention in more than 80% of TCGA patients.
source: Interestingly, we found several genes that were found as suitable points of intervention in most of the patients (MYC_MAX complex and SPOP were identified in more than 80% of the cases) (Appendix 1, Section 4.2, Appendix 1—figures 19 and 20), but others were specific to only some of the patients (MXI1 was identified in only 4 patients, 1% of the total, GLI in only 7% and WNT in 8% of patients).
evidence: This is a finding from the mutant analysis of personalized TCGA models.

claim: MXI1 was identified as a suitable point of intervention in only 4 patients (1% of the total).
source: Interestingly, we found several genes that were found as suitable points of intervention in most of the patients (MYC_MAX complex and SPOP were identified in more than 80% of the cases) (Appendix 1, Section 4.2, Appendix 1—figures 19 and 20), but others were specific to only some of the patients (MXI1 was identified in only 4 patients, 1% of the total, GLI in only 7% and WNT in 8% of patients).
evidence: This is a finding from the mutant analysis of personalized TCGA models.

claim: LNCaP was first isolated from a human metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma found in a lymph node.
source: LNCaP, first isolated from a human metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma found in a lymph node (Horoszewicz et al., 1983), is one of the most widely used cell lines for prostate cancer studies.
evidence: This is a historical fact about the LNCaP cell line, supported by citation.

claim: LNCaP is one of the most widely used cell lines for prostate cancer studies.
source: LNCaP, first isolated from a human metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma found in a lymph node (Horoszewicz et al., 1983), is one of the most widely used cell lines for prostate cancer studies.
evidence: This is a statement about the prevalence of LNCaP use in research.

claim: Androgen-sensitive LNCaP cells are representative of patients sensitive to treatments as opposed to resistant cell lines such as DU-145.
source: Androgen-sensitive LNCaP cells are representative of patients sensitive to treatments as opposed to resistant cell lines such as DU-145.
evidence: This is a characterization of LNCaP cells based on established knowledge.

claim: 32,258 mutants were analyzed for the LNCaP-specific model.
source: The analysis of the complete set of simulations for the 32,258 mutants can be found in the Appendix 1, Section 6.1 and in Supplementary file 6, where the LNCaP cell line-specific mutants and their phenotype scores are reported for all mutants.
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the mutant analysis performed.

claim: 29 nodes were identified as top knock-out mutations that depleted Proliferation or increased Apoptosis the most.
source: Among all combinations, we identified the top 20 knock-out mutations that depleted Proliferation or increased Apoptosis the most. As some of them overlapped, we ended up with 29 nodes: AKT, AR, ATR, AXIN1, Bak, BIRC5, CDH2, cFLAR, CyclinB, CyclinD, E2F1, eEF2K, eEF2, eEF2K, EGFR, ERK, HSPs, MED12, mTORC1, mTORC2, MYC, MYC_MAX, PHDs, PI3K, PIP3, SPOP, TAK1, TWIST1, and VHL.
evidence: This is a finding from the LNCaP mutant analysis.

claim: The Apoptosis score was slightly promoted when knocking out SPOP under all growth conditions.
source: Notably, the Apoptosis score was slightly promoted when knocking out SPOP under all growth conditions (Appendix 1, Section 7.3.1, Appendix 1—figure 35).
evidence: This is a simulation result from the LNCaP model.

claim: Proliferation depletion was accomplished when HSPs or MYC_MAX were inhibited under all conditions.
source: Likewise, Proliferation depletion was accomplished when HSPs or MYC_MAX were inhibited under all conditions and, less notably, when ERK, EGFR, SPOP, or PI3K were inhibited (Appendix 1, Section 7.3.1, Appendix 1—figure 35).
evidence: This is a simulation result from the LNCaP model.

claim: The combined inhibition of ERK and MYC_MAX nodes on the Proliferation score was synergistic.
source: We found that the combined inhibition of ERK and MYC_MAX nodes on the Proliferation score was synergistic (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the drug combination simulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The combined gradual inhibition of HSPs and PI3K nodes affects the Proliferation score in a joint manner with some Bliss Independence synergy.
source: Another synergistic pair is the combined gradual inhibition of HSPs and PI3K nodes that also affects the Proliferation score in a joint manner (Figure 5B), with some Bliss Independence synergy found (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from the drug combination simulations shown in Figures 5B and 5D.

claim: LNCaP is more sensitive to drugs targeting AKT or TERT than the rest of the studied prostate cell lines.
source: We observed that LNCaP is more sensitive to drugs targeting AKT or TERT than the rest of the studied prostate cell lines.
evidence: This is an observation from the GDSC drug sensitivity data analysis.

claim: LNCaP cell lines are especially sensitive to drugs targeting PI3K/AKT/mTOR, hormone-related (AR targeting) and Chromatin (bromodomain inhibitors, regulating Myc) pathways.
source: For instance, target enrichment analysis showed that LNCaP cell lines are especially sensitive to drugs targeting PI3K/AKT/mTOR, hormone-related (AR targeting) and Chromatin (bromodomain inhibitors, regulating Myc) pathways (adjusted p-values from target enrichment: 0.001, 0.001, and 0.032, respectively, Appendix 1, Section 7.1, Appendix 1—table 2), which corresponds to the model predictions (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from target enrichment analysis with statistical support.

claim: The LNCaP cell line is more sensitive to drugs targeting model-identified nodes than to drugs targeting other proteins (Mann-Whitney U p-value 0.00041).
source: Also, the LNCaP cell line is more sensitive to drugs targeting model-identified nodes than to drugs targeting other proteins (Appendix 1, Section 7.1, Appendix 1—figure 32, Mann-Whitney U p-value 0.00041), and this effect is specific for LNCaP cell line (Mann-Whitney U p-values ranging from 0.0033 to 0.38 for other prostate cancer cell lines).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the drug sensitivity analysis.

claim: Hsp90 (NMS-E973, 17-DMAG) and PI3K/AKT pathway (PI-103, Pictilisib) inhibitors showed a dose-dependent activity in the endpoint cell viability assay after 48 hr incubation.
source: Notably, Hsp90 (NMS-E973,17-DMAG) and PI3K/AKT pathway (PI-103, Pictilisib) inhibitors showed a dose-dependent activity in the endpoint cell viability assay determined by the fluorescent resazurin after a 48 hr incubation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 7.

claim: Dose-dependent activity is more notable in Hsp90 drugs (NMS-E973, 17-DMAG) than in PI3K/AKT pathway (Pictilisib) ones and very modest for PI-103.
source: This dose-dependent activity is more notable in Hsp90 drugs (NMS-E973,17-DMAG) than in PI3K/AKT pathway (Pictilisib) ones and very modest for PI-103.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental results in Figure 7.

claim: Both Hsp90 inhibitors tested, 17-DMAG and NMS-E973, reduced the cell viability 12 hr after drug supplementation.
source: Both Hsp90 inhibitors tested, 17-DMAG and NMS-E973, reduced the cell viability 12 hr after drug supplementation (Figure 8A for 17-DMAG and Figure 8B for NMS-E973), with 17-DMAG having a stronger effect and in a more clear concentration-dependent manner than NMS-E973 (Appendix 1, Section 8, Appendix 1—figure 40, panels B-D for 17-DMAG and panels F-H for NMS-E973).
evidence: This is an experimental result from the RT-CES assay shown in Figure 8.

claim: 17-DMAG had a stronger effect and in a more clear concentration-dependent manner than NMS-E973.
source: Both Hsp90 inhibitors tested, 17-DMAG and NMS-E973, reduced the cell viability 12 hr after drug supplementation (Figure 8A for 17-DMAG and Figure 8B for NMS-E973), with 17-DMAG having a stronger effect and in a more clear concentration-dependent manner than NMS-E973 (Appendix 1, Section 8, Appendix 1—figure 40, panels B-D for 17-DMAG and panels F-H for NMS-E973).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the experimental results.

claim: Both PI3K/AKT pathway inhibitors tested, Pictilisib and PI-103, reduced the cell viability immediately after drug supplementation.
source: Likewise, both PI3K/AKT pathway inhibitors tested, Pictilisib and PI-103, reduced the cell viability immediately after drug supplementation (Figure 9A for Pictilisib and Figure 9B for PI-103), in a concentration-dependent manner (Appendix 1, Section 8, Appendix 1—figure 41B-D, for Pictilisib and panels F-H for PI-103).
evidence: This is an experimental result from the RT-CES assay shown in Figure 9.

claim: Hsp90 inhibitors had a more prolonged effect on the cells' proliferation than PI3K/AKT pathway inhibitors.
source: In addition, Hsp90 inhibitors had a more prolonged effect on the cells' proliferation than PI3K/AKT pathway inhibitors.
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the experimental results.

claim: The Hsp90 chaperone is expressed abundantly and plays a crucial role in the correct folding of a wide variety of proteins such as protein kinases and steroid hormone receptors.
source: The Hsp90 chaperone is expressed abundantly and plays a crucial role in the correct folding of a wide variety of proteins such as protein kinases and steroid hormone receptors (Schopf et al., 2017).
evidence: This is background information about Hsp90, supported by citation.

claim: Hsp90 can act as a protector of less stable proteins produced by DNA mutations in cancer cells.
source: Hsp90 can act as a protector of less stable proteins produced by DNA mutations in cancer cells (Barrott and Haystead, 2013; Hessenkemper and Baniahmad, 2013).
evidence: This is background information about Hsp90, supported by citations.

claim: Hsp90 inhibitors are in clinical trials for multiple indications in cancer.
source: Currently, Hsp90 inhibitors are in clinical trials for multiple indications in cancer (Chen et al., 2020; Iwai et al., 2012; Le et al., 2017).
evidence: This is background information about Hsp90 inhibitors, supported by citations.

claim: The PI3K/AKT signalling pathway controls many different cellular processes such as cell growth, motility, proliferation, and apoptosis and is frequently altered in different cancer cells.
source: The PI3K/AKT signalling pathway controls many different cellular processes such as cell growth, motility, proliferation, and apoptosis and is frequently altered in different cancer cells (Carceles-Cordon et al., 2020; Shorning et al., 2020).
evidence: This is background information about the PI3K/AKT pathway, supported by citations.

claim: Many PI3K/AKT inhibitors are in different stages of clinical development, and some of them are approved for clinical use.
source: Many PI3K/AKT inhibitors are in different stages of clinical development, and some of them are approved for clinical use (Table 1).
evidence: This is background information about PI3K/AKT inhibitors, with reference to Table 1.

claim: The final model includes pathways such as androgen receptor, MAPK, Wnt, NFkB, PI3K/AKT, MAPK, mTOR, SHH, the cell cycle, the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), apoptosis and DNA damage pathways.
source: The final network includes pathways such as androgen receptor, MAPK, Wnt, NFkB, PI3K/AKT, MAPK, mTOR, SHH, the cell cycle, the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), apoptosis and DNA damage pathways.
evidence: This describes the pathways included in the final model.

claim: The most frequent fusion gene in prostate cancer is TMPRSS2:ERG.
source: The most frequent is TMPRSS2:ERG, as it involves the transcription factor ERG, which leads to cell-cycle progression.
evidence: This is a statement about prostate cancer genetics based on established knowledge.

claim: ERG fuses with the AR-regulated TMPRSS2 gene promoter to form an oncogenic fusion gene that is especially common in hormone-refractory prostate cancer.
source: ERG fuses with the AR-regulated TMPRSS2 gene promoter to form an oncogenic fusion gene that is especially common in hormone-refractory prostate cancer, conferring androgen responsiveness to ERG.
evidence: This is a statement about the TMPRSS2:ERG fusion based on established knowledge.

claim: ERG directly regulates EZH2, oncogene c-Myc and many other targets in prostate cancer.
source: A literature search reveals that ERG directly regulates EZH2, oncogene c-Myc and many other targets in prostate cancer (Kunderfranco et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about ERG function, supported by citation.

claim: Loss of NKX3-1 favours recruitment to the ERG gene breakpoint of proteins that promote error-prone non-homologous end-joining.
source: Thus, loss of NKX3-1 favours recruitment to the ERG gene breakpoint of proteins that promote error-prone non-homologous end-joining (Bowen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about NKX3-1 function, supported by citation.

claim: Publicly available data of 489 human prostate cancer patients from TCGA were used in the present work.
source: Publicly available data of 489 human prostate cancer patients from TCGA described in Hoadley et al., 2018 were used in the present work.
evidence: This describes the data source used in the study.

claim: 488 samples had complete omics datasets after data gathering.
source: We gathered mutations, CNA, RNA and clinical data from cBioPortal (https://www.cbioportal.org/study/summary?id=prad_tcga_pan_can_atlas_2018) for all of these samples resulting in 488 with complete omics datasets.
evidence: This describes the final dataset used after filtering.

claim: 17-DMAG is an Hsp90 inhibitor with an IC50 of 62 nM in a cell-free assay.
source: 17-DMAG is an Hsp90 inhibitor with an IC50 of 62 nM in a cell-free assay (Pacey et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a characterization of the drug, supported by citation.

claim: NMS-E973 is an Hsp90 inhibitor with DC50 of <10 nM for Hsp90 binding.
source: NMS-E973 is an Hsp90 inhibitor with DC50 of <10 nM for Hsp90 binding (Fogliatto et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a characterization of the drug, supported by citation.

claim: The model was deposited in the GINsim Database with identifier 252.
source: This model was deposited in the GINsim Database with identifier 252 (http://ginsim.org/model/signalling-prostate-cancer) and in BioModels (Malik-Sheriff et al., 2020) with identifier MODEL2106070001 (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biomodels/MODEL2106070001).
evidence: This describes where the model has been deposited for public access.

claim: The model was deposited in BioModels with identifier MODEL2106070001.
source: This model was deposited in the GINsim Database with identifier 252 (http://ginsim.org/model/signalling-prostate-cancer) and in BioModels (Malik-Sheriff et al., 2020) with identifier MODEL2106070001 (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biomodels/MODEL2106070001).
evidence: This describes where the model has been deposited for public access.
